w: What's tested Dr. Herr's study guide for this lecture: disorders of testicular development and descent (cryptorchidism), the major categories of testicular tumors (germ cell tumors, 95 percent, against the sex cord-stromal tumors; seminoma against the non-seminomatous tumors), the common infections of the male reproductive tract, and the major benign and malignant prostate disorders (BPH, prostatic adenocarcinoma and its Gleason grading) Her two closing reminders: "cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer," and phimosis is a predisposing factor to carcinoma of the penis HPV in the male genital tract: condyloma acuminatum is benign, from the low-risk types 6 and 11; penile intraepithelial neoplasia comes from the high-risk types 16 and 18 ("the lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign; higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant"), or, in older men, without HPV, from lichen sclerosus The prostate's zones predict its disease: BPH around the urethra, which obstructs the urine; carcinoma in the peripheral zone, which spreads to bone and makes it (osteoblastic), with PSA in the blood The bladder: the urothelium, the benign conditions (congenital anomalies, reflux, diverticula, stones, cystitis), and urothelial carcinoma: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors, most of them in the bladder, with smoking the strongest risk factor What the lecture said you don't need: the WHO classifications of urinary tract and testicular tumors, the two molecular pathways of urothelial carcinoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis, the seminoma's look under the microscope, and the details of each non-seminomatous tumor ("you just need to know seminomatous versus non-seminomatous") Dr. Dal Zotto, a pathologist originally from Argentina, gave Lecture 21 on Wednesday, November 18, at 1 pm, the first part of a two-hour session that went on to the female reproductive system (Lecture 22) after a break. The deck, "Pathology of Lower Urinary Tract and Male Reproductive System", starts with the urinary collecting system and the bladder, then takes the male organs one at a time: the penis, the testis and the prostate. Dr. Dal Zotto warned that it would be "a little heavy" and kept telling the class which parts are only for general information. These notes follow the recording. These notes are written from the recording. The slides were posted the same day but couldn't be opened for this update yet, so a detail that is only on a slide (one not read aloud) isn't here. The recording's captions name every speaker "Michael Herr", the room's Zoom account. The urinary collecting system The urinary collecting system is every tube and organ that collects the urine the kidneys make and carries it out: inside the kidney, the renal pelvis and calyces; the two ureters, long retroperitoneal tubes, one on each side; the bladder, a single pelvic organ shaped like an inverted pear; and the urethra, short in women and longer in men. All of it is lined by one epithelium, the urothelium (its old name is transitional epithelium), except the distal urethra: it opens onto the perineal skin and is lined by non-keratinizing squamous epithelium, like the skin. Under the urothelium are the submucosa (supporting tissue, vessels and nerves) and the muscularis propria, smooth muscle that helps pump the urine along; in the bladder it is very thick. The urothelium Urothelial cells sit in 5 to 7 layers, with oval nuclei perpendicular to the basement membrane. On top are the umbrella cells: big cells with ample cytoplasm, connected to each other, the ones in contact with the urine. "Urine is toxic, guys," Dr. Dal Zotto said: the epithelium has to be strong to stand urine's high levels of nitrogen. Benign conditions of the ureters and bladder Congenital anomalies (from fetal development): a double ureter, on one side or both, which may insert into the bladder separately or fuse before it does. They're benign, but they can obstruct the urine and cause hydronephrosis. Vesicoureteral reflux: the muscle where the ureter inserts into the bladder is malformed, so when the bladder contracts, urine goes back up the ureter instead of out. In children it causes repeated urinary tract infections and infections that ascend to the kidneys. Exstrophy of the bladder: the abdominal wall doesn't form, so the bladder is exposed to the outside; it is corrected with surgery. Diverticula, especially of the bladder (next). Ureteral obstruction, much more common: stones (calculi), very painful, lodge at narrow, weak points, especially where the ureter inserts into the bladder, on one side or both; a tumor growing inside can obstruct too. (Retroperitoneal fibrosis: "forget about that.") Cystitis, very common: acute and chronic bacterial cystitis, from skin bacteria ascending the urethra to the bladder; and non-infectious cystitis, from drugs or radiation. Bladder diverticulum Weak spots in the bladder's muscle let the mucosa and submucosa pouch outward (an evagination) into the soft tissue around the bladder when the pressure inside it rises. A diverticulum is a serious problem because it can become infected, and carcinoma can develop in it later. Bladder cancer Bladder cancer is the fourth most common cancer in men (prostate cancer is first). In women it ranks below 10th or 15th, so it is mostly a disease of men, usually white, non-Hispanic patients, though Black patients have the worst prognosis when it occurs. It is about 5 percent of U.S. cancer diagnoses. It doesn't cause as many deaths as lung, prostate, colorectal or pancreatic cancer, because it behaves well and is well controlled: surgery, cystoscopy and surveillance with urine cytology. But it is one of the most expensive cancers to treat, because once diagnosed, the patient needs surveillance for life. The lecture also called it "the fourth cause of death in men" right after saying it doesn't cause many deaths; the ranking given first is among cancers diagnosed in men. No question here depends on its rank as a cause of death. Urothelial carcinoma "You just need to know" that most urinary tract tumors come from the urothelium: 90 percent are urothelial carcinomas, and most of them are in the bladder. "If you remember only that the majority of the urothelial neoplasms are located in the bladder and are urothelial carcinomas, I will be happy." Less common are squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and benign or malignant mesenchymal tumors of the wall. The WHO classification isn't needed. Urothelial carcinoma can arise anywhere urothelium lines the tract, the bladder most often, and usually in adult men. Its symptoms are easy to overlook: minimal hematuria and no pain for years, until it obstructs or causes pain. Risk factors for urothelial carcinoma Smoking, the strongest: urothelial carcinoma is four times more frequent in smokers, and unlike lung cancer, the risk doesn't go down after quitting. Occupational exposures: work with rubber, leather, textiles and dyes (anilines, beta-naphthylamine) and paints. Pelvic radiation: women treated with radiation for cervical cancer can later develop bladder carcinoma, the special setting where the lecture said it is seen in women. Drugs such as cyclophosphamide, and chronic catheters and infections. Schistosoma haematobium, a parasite: a frequent cause of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in Africa, especially Egypt ("if you have patients that are coming from Egypt, you can relate"). Papillary tumors, grade and stage Urothelial carcinomas are papillary or non-papillary, and low or high grade; they can invade the stroma and become invasive carcinomas. The lecture showed the two molecular pathways behind them (FGFR3 mutations in the papillary ones, TP53 in the non-papillary ones) as "just your general information. You don't need to know." A non-invasive papillary urothelial carcinoma has finger-like (villous) projections into the urinary space. In a low-grade one the nuclei are uniform, nearly all the same size; in a high-grade one there is nuclear pleomorphism, nuclei of different sizes and shapes. To the eye, papillary tumors are exophytic: bumpy, verrucous growths into the bladder. The prognosis depends on the histology and on the stage. The American Joint Committee on Cancer stages it by how deep it goes into the bladder wall: superficial, into the muscularis propria, or beyond it into other tissues, such as the prostate just below the bladder. The deeper it goes, the higher the stage and the worse the prognosis. The male reproductive system Its organs: the penis, the prostate below the bladder, the seminal vesicles, the vas deferens and the testis. "Males are complicated," Dr. Dal Zotto said: a lot of organs. Hypospadias and epispadias The urethra normally opens at the tip of the glans. In hypospadias it opens on the ventral side of the penis (underneath); in epispadias, on the dorsal side (on top). They are usually found with other anomalies of the newborn's genital tract, and the angles in the urethra can obstruct the flow of urine. Phimosis Phimosis is a foreskin so tight over the glans that it can't be retracted when it needs to be. It is very common in toddlers. If the foreskin isn't retracted and cleaned, the fold fills with smegma (shed squamous cells and secretions), which gets stiff and predisposes to infection, chronic inflammation and eventually carcinoma of the penis. The closing reminder: phimosis is a predisposing factor to penile carcinoma. Infections of the penis Infection of the glans and prepuce (the foreskin) is either nonspecific, such as bacterial, or a specific sexually transmitted disease: syphilis, gonorrhea or chlamydia. Condyloma acuminatum A benign, sexually transmitted lesion, not only of the penis but of the whole anogenital skin: the perineum, the vulva, the anus and the perianal skin. It is caused by HPV types 6 and 11, which are called low risk because they don't predispose to cancer. It looks white and verrucous (wart-like), around the coronal sulcus, on the glans and on the inner foreskin. It is very contagious, and even without lesions the virus stays latent in the mucosa and can still be transmitted. Penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) The premalignant lesion, the one that can turn into squamous cell carcinoma, comes in two kinds: HPV-associated, the more frequent: from the high-risk types, 16 and 18. "So remember, the lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign. Higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant." HPV-independent: in older men (over 60) with chronic inflammation of the foreskin and glans, an atrophic epithelium and lichen sclerosus; the less frequent kind. "Look at this number": 30 percent progress to invasive carcinoma if they're not treated. PeIN looks nothing like a condyloma: it is flat and reddish, looks ulcerated and can ulcerate, and isn't exophytic or verrucous. Under the microscope it is a proliferation confined to the squamous epithelium, non-invasive but able to invade the stroma: a low-grade lesion still matures somewhat and resembles the normal mucosa; a high-grade one looks immature. Cause HPV 6 and 11 (low risk) HPV 16 and 18 (high risk) No HPV: chronic inflammation, atrophy, lichen sclerosus Behavior Benign, sexually transmitted, contagious Premalignant: 30 percent invasive if untreated Premalignant Who Any age, sexually active The more frequent kind Older men, over 60 Look White, verrucous, exophytic Flat, reddish, may ulcerate Flat, with an atrophic epithelium Squamous cell carcinoma of the penis Not frequent in the United States, more common in developing countries and in patients of lower socioeconomic status: poor hygiene, phimosis and chronic inflammation of the foreskin predispose to HPV infection and then carcinoma. Its course is indolent: it can spread to the inguinal lymph nodes but not much further. The heaviest burden is the psychological stigma of a tumor of the genitals. In a partial penectomy specimen cut along its length you see the urethra, surrounded by the corpus spongiosum, the corpus cavernosum on the dorsal side, and the tumor: exophytic, a bumpy, cauliflower-like growth, here on the dorsal glans, invading the stroma under it. Under the microscope an invasive carcinoma is irregular nests of squamous cells going into the stroma; carcinoma in situ (PeIN) stays within the epithelium. The testis The testis hangs in the scrotum for a reason: spermatogenesis "likes cool weather," and the scrotum keeps the testes about 2 degrees below body temperature. Its coverings are the tunica vaginalis, an extension of the peritoneum from the abdomen, and the testis's own capsule, the tunica albuginea ("alba means white, and it is really white"). At the back is the rete testis, a network of tubules, with the vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The sperm leave through the epididymis, on the back of the testis, and the vas deferens, which carries them on to the urethra. The spermatic cord is wrapped in fat and soft tissue. The cut testis is brown and a little granular, because it is packed with seminiferous tubules. They hold two kinds of cells: the germ cells, spermatogonia, which mature into spermatids in cycles of about 70 days, and the Sertoli cells, which conduct that maturation through the hormones they secrete. Outside the tubules are the Leydig cells, bigger, plump cells with granular cytoplasm that secrete testosterone. Sertoli and Leydig cells aren't germ cells: they are the sex cord-stromal cells. The lecture said Leydig cells secrete testosterone and dihydrotestosterone. Most dihydrotestosterone is made from testosterone in the target tissues, by 5-alpha-reductase (Lecture 18); no question here depends on it. The lecture also said the vas deferens "ends up in the ureter": it joins the urethra, through the ejaculatory duct in the prostate. Benign conditions of the scrotum and testis Hydrocele: fluid collecting between the two layers of the tunica vaginalis, a common cause of swelling, for example from obstructed lymphatic flow in older men, but in young men too. Epididymitis: inflammation of the epididymis, from sexually transmitted gonorrhea or chlamydia, or a nonspecific urinary tract infection that spreads to it. Orchitis: inflammation of the testis itself, which is very uncommon: viral, syphilis (Treponema pallidum), tuberculosis, brucellosis and other causes. Two emergencies: torsion and inguinal hernia Testicular torsion: a loose spermatic cord twists in the inguinal canal and cuts off the testis's blood supply, which can lead to infarction. Losing one testis won't make a man infertile (there's another), but torsion is a medical emergency. Inguinal hernia: the testes start out retroperitoneal before birth and descend through the inguinal canal, which can still be open in the first years of life. A loop of intestine can slip into the canal and get trapped: sudden pain on one side of the groin, and an emergency, because that segment of bowel can infarct. Cryptorchidism "Crypto means hidden": in cryptorchidism a testis is hidden, not in the scrotum. The testes develop retroperitoneally and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum before birth; the lecture said about 1 in 10 newborns have at least one undescended testis. The clinician waits through the first year, up to the second, for it to come down; if it hasn't come down by about 2 years old, it needs surgery. Why: the retroperitoneum and the inguinal canal are at body temperature, 37 °C, and that heat halts spermatogenesis, leading to infertility and testicular cancer. Correcting it surgically prevents the infertility, but "the risk of testicular cancer is still a possibility for that kid." The closing reminder: cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer. The two figures are the lecture's: textbooks put undescended testes at about 3 percent of full-term newborn boys (more in preterm ones), and current guidelines correct them by about 18 months. No question here depends on either number. Testicular atrophy, as in infertility, looks like this under the microscope: no spermatids and no spermatogonia in the seminiferous tubules, only Sertoli cells, and a thickened basement membrane. Testicular tumors 95 percent of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia. The rest are sex cord-stromal tumors (from the Sertoli and Leydig cells) or mixed tumors, and in older men, lymphoma (involving the testis secondarily, not starting there) and metastases. The incidence differs from country to country and, unlike penile cancer, isn't tied to low socioeconomic status; no one knows the factors. Norway has the highest incidence, and Hispanic men have a high incidence too. Germ cell tumors are cured in more than 95 percent of cases, so in general they behave well. The risk factor to know is cryptorchidism. Seminoma versus non-seminomatous germ cell tumors You don't need the classification, Dr. Dal Zotto said; for you it "is going to be simple": seminoma versus non-seminomatous tumors. The split matters because seminoma behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy, and the rest don't respond as well. "So the clinician needs to know if this is a seminoma or a non-seminomatous tumor, and that's enough." Seminoma, the most frequent: white, multinodular and solid, with no hemorrhage and no necrosis. A tumor of young adults, in their 30s and 40s ("if I see a young adult with a testicular tumor, I'm going to think, okay, this has a high chance to be a seminoma"). It is associated with cryptorchidism and usually has no serum tumor marker the clinician can measure, so it needs a pathologist to make the diagnosis. Non-seminomatous tumors: a germ cell can give rise to any tissue in the body, so these recapitulate the tissues of fetal life: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma. They are more aggressive than seminoma, and choriocarcinoma most of all. Dr. Dal Zotto called the rest "general information" you don't need: the seminoma's clear cells in nests that look like fried eggs; embryonal carcinoma's hemorrhage, necrosis and variegated cut surface; the yolk sac tumor's cysts and Schiller-Duval bodies; choriocarcinoma's trophoblast-like cells, which make beta-hCG and metastasize early; and the teratoma's mature tissues (cartilage, glands, skin) or immature neuroepithelium. No question here asks for them. Members Seminoma Embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma Frequency The most frequent Less frequent Cut surface White, multinodular, solid; no hemorrhage or necrosis Often hemorrhage and necrosis Behavior Behaves very well More aggressive Radiotherapy Responds Doesn't respond as well Serum markers Usually none: the pathologist diagnoses it Some make them (choriocarcinoma: beta-hCG) The prostate A little gland of about 20 grams, below the bladder. The urethra runs through it, and it connects with the seminal vesicles and the ejaculatory ducts. It makes glycoproteins, such as prostate-specific antigen (PSA), that keep the sperm nourished and moving until they reach their destination. Its zones predict its disease. The part around the urethra (the transition, or periurethral, zone) is where benign prostatic hyperplasia arises; the peripheral zone, toward the back, is where prostatic carcinoma arises. Because BPH grows around the urethra, it obstructs the urine; a carcinoma out in the periphery doesn't. The lecture called the periurethral part the "central zone" and, in the same breath, the "transitional zone". In anatomy texts BPH arises in the transition zone, around the urethra, and the central zone is a separate zone around the ejaculatory ducts. The questions here say "around the urethra" or "transition zone". Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) Hyperplasia of both the glands and the stroma of the prostate, around the urethra, so it obstructs the urethra and the flow of urine. It is very common: "Guys, you are going to have it. You cannot avoid this. After 50s, your prostate is going to start to be hyperplastic." The result is difficulty urinating. Hormonal factors play a role, and surgery treats the severe obstructive cases. Prostatic adenocarcinoma The most frequent cancer in men, a tumor of older men (over 65), arising in the peripheral zone. It is easy to diagnose because it has a marker, PSA, measured in the serum by a simple blood draw: the lecture said the glands of a prostatic adenocarcinoma make 10 times more PSA than normal glands, and that men over 50 have their PSA checked as surveillance. "The one thing that the prostatic adenocarcinoma does very special is that it likes the bones": it metastasizes to bone, and the metastases characteristically form more bone, so they are called osteoblastic. An osteoblastic bone lesion in a man means thinking of prostatic adenocarcinoma and ordering a PSA. The prognosis depends on how differentiated it is, graded with the Gleason grading system: from well-differentiated glands to poorly differentiated masses of tumor and single cells. The worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis. Where Around the urethra (transition, periurethral zone) Peripheral zone, toward the back What grows Glands and stroma, benign Malignant glands Urine Obstructs it: difficulty urinating Doesn't obstruct it Who Nearly every man, starting after 50 Older men, over 65; the most frequent cancer in men Found by The symptoms Serum PSA Spread None: benign Bone, osteoblastic Grading None Gleason, from well to poorly differentiated The review at the end: "Remember, cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer," and phimosis, a foreskin that can't retract, "is a predisposing factor to penile carcinoma."
